title: Psalm 57: In the Shadow of Your Wings
summary: Hiding in a cave from Saul, David takes refuge in God's shadow while enemies surround him like lions. Twice a refrain asks God to be exalted above the heavens. The psalm ends in morning praise, with David waking his harp to sing of God's love and faithfulness among the nations.
story: Psalm 57 follows directly from Psalm 56 and shares its label (Miktam) and its opening cry for mercy. Psalm 56 placed David in Philistine Gath; this one places him back in Judah, hiding in a cave from Saul. The two psalms together trace the years in which David, already anointed by Samuel, lived as a fugitive while the reigning king tried to kill him. Here the mood lifts further than in Psalm 56: the second half is almost entirely praise. Its closing verses (7 to 11) were reused, with small changes, as the opening of Psalm 108, which shows that Israel's singers treated such psalms as living material for later worship.
historical:
The heading says David wrote it “when he fled from Saul into the cave.” Two caves appear in David's story. In 1 Samuel 22:1 he escaped to the cave of Adullam, in the lowlands of Judah, where his family and a band of distressed and indebted men gathered around him. In 1 Samuel 24 he hid in a cave near En-gedi, by the Dead Sea, and Saul walked in alone; David cut off a corner of the king's robe but refused to harm the LORD's anointed. Psalm 142 also names a cave. Interpreters differ on which cave is meant here, and the heading doesn't say. Verse 6, where the enemies fall into their own pit, fits the En-gedi episode especially well, since Saul came into the very place where he could have been killed.

As with the other historical headings in the Psalter, scholars disagree about whether the note records the original occasion or is an early editorial link to the Samuel narrative. The tune name, “Do Not Destroy,” also heads Psalms 58, 59, and 75. Its meaning is unknown, though some connect it with David's words to Abishai, do not destroy him, when he spared Saul a second time (1 Samuel 26:9). That link is a guess and not more.
cultural:
The shadow of wings was a familiar picture of protection. A mother bird shelters her young under her wings, and Boaz uses the same picture when he blesses Ruth for coming to take refuge under the wings of Israel's God (Ruth 2:12). Many interpreters also hear an allusion to the outstretched wings of the cherubim over the ark of the covenant in the tabernacle's inner room, the place of God's presence. Either way, refuge in God is described in terms of a place where one can hide.

Lions were a real danger in ancient Israel, living in the thickets of the Jordan valley and the wilderness, and they became a stock image for violent enemies. The harp and lyre of verse 8 were the stringed instruments of Israel's worship, played by Levites in the temple and by David himself at Saul's court (1 Samuel 16:23). In a world without artificial light, dawn was the time when the day's work and prayer began. David's claim that he will “awaken the dawn” reverses the usual order: instead of the sun waking the singer, the singer's praise wakes the day.
literary: The psalm has two halves, each closed by the same refrain: “Be exalted, O God, above the heavens; may Your glory cover all the earth” (verses 5 and 11). The first half (verses 1 to 5) is a prayer for refuge amid danger. The second (verses 6 to 11) turns on the enemies' failure, since they fall into their own pit, and moves into praise. Repetition drives the poem: the opening doubles “have mercy,” verse 7 doubles “my heart is steadfast,” and verse 8 repeats the call to awake. The enemies are described with violent images of mouths (teeth like spears, tongues like swords), which the refrain answers with the image of God's glory covering the whole earth. Two Selah notes mark pauses; the word's meaning is uncertain, perhaps a musical interlude.

outline.t: Refuge under God's wings and a cry to God Most High
Surrounded by lions and sharp tongues
Refrain: be exalted above the heavens
The trap-setters fall into their own pit
A steadfast heart wakes the dawn with praise
Refrain: may Your glory cover all the earth

doctrines.note: David calls on God Most High, “who fulfills His purpose for me.” Even while he hides in a cave, he trusts that God's purpose for his life will be completed and that the enemies' traps will turn on themselves.

The psalm pairs God's loving devotion and his faithfulness twice (verses 3 and 10). These two qualities, his committed covenant love and his reliability, are the grounds of David's confidence and the content of his praise.
A hunted man in a cave vows to praise God “among the nations.” The refrain asks that God's glory cover all the earth. Israel's worship, even in private distress, looks outward to the whole world.

words.note: Chasah, to seek refuge. It is one of the key verbs of the Psalter, appearing from Psalm 2:12 onward. It describes running to a shelter and staying there. In verse 1 the soul takes refuge in God and under the shadow of his wings: the refuge is a person, not a place.

Chesed, loving devotion, steadfast love, covenant kindness. It is the loyal love God has pledged to his people, joined here with emet, faithfulness. In verse 3 God sends them out like messengers to rescue David; in verse 10 they reach to the heavens and clouds. The word is hard to render with one English word because it combines love, loyalty, and mercy.

Kun, to be established or firm. Verse 7 says “My heart is steadfast,” a heart fixed and set in place. The same verb is used of God establishing thrones and the earth itself. David's steadiness in the cave is not natural calm but a heart fastened on God.

Kavod, glory. The word's root carries the sense of weight or heaviness, and it came to mean honor, splendor, and the visible presence of God. The refrain prays that God's glory will cover all the earth, the same hope voiced in Numbers 14:21 and Habakkuk 2:14.

christ: Jesus used the image of verse 1 when he grieved over Jerusalem: he had longed to gather its children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings (Matthew 23:37). What the psalm says of God's protection, Jesus offered in his own person. David in the cave, spared from Saul and sparing Saul in turn, is a king rejected before he reigns, a pattern the Gospels see fulfilled in Jesus, the anointed king who was hunted and rejected before he was exalted. The vow to praise God among the nations anticipates the mission to the Gentiles that Paul describes in Romans 15:8-12, where he quotes other psalms with the same hope. These are thematic and typological links rather than direct predictions.
questions: David wrote this psalm while hiding in a cave. What is your cave right now, and what would it mean to take refuge in God there?
What does it mean to have a steadfast heart when circumstances are anything but steady?
David wants to praise God “among the nations.” How can your private experience of God's help become something that blesses others?
